article.overview: A radiation environment monitoring package is an instrument or small instrument set that measures the ionising radiation present at a location on or around the Moon. It records how much energy radiation deposits in a detector (absorbed dose), what kinds of particles are present (charged particles, neutrons, heavy ions) and how these quantities change with time. Lunar radiation comes mainly from galactic cosmic rays and from solar energetic particles. The Moon has no global magnetic field or thick atmosphere to slow these particles, so the radiation reaching the surface is strongly influenced by the lunar body itself. The examples documented here are flown instruments: the Cosmic Ray Telescope for the Effects of Radiation (CRaTER) on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), the Lunar Lander Neutron and Dosimetry (LND) experiment on China's Chang'e-4 lander, and the Radiation Dose Monitor (RADOM) on India's Chandrayaan-1 orbiter. Each is a different design flown in a different environment, and their values must not be compared as if they were the same instrument.
article.description: A radiation environment monitoring package usually combines three things: radiation sensors, electronics that count and classify each particle interaction, and a time reference so that data can be compared with solar activity or spacecraft position. Sensors are most often silicon solid-state detectors, which produce an electrical pulse when a charged particle passes through them; the pulse size indicates the energy deposited. Some designs add neutron-sensitive material, such as gadolinium conversion foil, because neutrons do not produce signals in silicon by themselves. The term 'package' does not describe one fixed design. Some packages are a single sensor head on an orbiter; others are a sensor head plus an electronics box inside a lander; some are passive dosimeters read after exposure. The published examples here are all active electronic instruments.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Characterising the radiation field: orbital and surface measurements show how dose rate varies with orbit altitude, lunar day and night, and solar activity. The LND paper states that radiation measurements near the Moon were 'remarkably scarce' before the Chang'e-4 mission, and that surface data relied on calculations (Wimmer-Schweingruber et al., 2020). Radiation risk to crews and biology: measured dose and particle-type information are inputs to models that estimate biological effects; the LND paper states its measurements are relevant to astronauts on the lunar surface or in lunar orbit. This record does not provide a risk assessment. Neutron environment and subsurface composition: surface neutron measurements can be related to hydrogen content and regolith composition; LND includes thermal-neutron detection for this reason (Wimmer-Schweingruber et al., 2020). Calibrating and validating models: radiation transport models of the Moon, Earth-orbit environments and spacecraft shielding depend on measured reference data. Supporting human-spaceflight planning: long-term dose records can inform shielding design, mission duration limits and activity timing during solar events. These uses are described in the cited literature as motivations; no specific operational use by a mission is documented in the sources reviewed.
article.operating_principle: Charged-particle telescope: CRaTER and LND both use stacks of silicon detectors arranged as particle telescopes. A charged particle passing through several detectors leaves a signal in each one; comparing the energy deposited in each layer allows the instrument to estimate the particle's Linear Energy Transfer (LET), the energy deposited per unit distance travelled in a material. LET is a key quantity because it determines how strongly a particle damages biological tissue or electronics (Wilson et al., cited in Wimmer-Schweingruber et al., 2020). Tissue-equivalent shielding: CRaTER places tissue-equivalent plastic between detector pairs, so the detectors behind it respond in a configuration that approximates dose to tissue (UNH CRaTER instrument description). Absorbed dose and dose equivalent: the LND instrument measures absorbed dose in silicon, which does not directly measure tissue-equivalent dose. Conversion to a biologically weighted dose equivalent requires a quality factor (Q) for each particle type and energy, using ICRP 103 recommendations (Wimmer-Schweingruber et al., 2020). Neutron detection: thermal neutrons deposit little energy in silicon directly. The LND design places a 20 micrometre gadolinium conversion foil between silicon detector pairs (E and F, and G and H); thermal neutrons react with gadolinium, producing secondary particles detected by the adjacent silicon detectors. Electronics and timing: each detector pulse is amplified, shaped and digitised; the electronics box classifies events and accumulates counts over preset intervals, with thermal-neutron counts at 10 minutes, high-resolution data at 1 hour and dose-rate time series at up to 1-minute cadence (Wimmer-Schweingruber et al., 2020).
article.scientific_importance: Radiation at the Moon differs from the environment in low Earth orbit. The Earth's magnetic field deflects many cosmic rays and shields the planet's surface; on the Moon the surface is directly exposed for the whole lunar day, and the body itself blocks radiation from one direction at a time. Measurements of this environment therefore support both space-environment science and engineering. The LND surface result, published as 'First measurements of the radiation dose on the lunar surface' (Zhang et al., 2020), is the first direct measurement of radiation dose on the lunar surface in the literature reviewed here. Previous surface estimates were model-based. Surface measurements include the effects of the lunar body, the lander and the local environment, which orbital data alone cannot capture. Orbital data from CRaTER and RADOM remain important for understanding the radiation environment across altitudes and solar conditions; the LND paper compares its context against these earlier orbital results (Wimmer-Schweingruber et al., 2020).

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power requirement for a radiation environment monitoring package. The three examples have different architectures (CRaTER and RADOM on orbiters, LND on a lander) and values apply only to the named instrument. Where a value is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed, this is stated as null or 'not publicly specified'.

examples.name: Cosmic Ray Telescope for the Effects of Radiation (CRaTER), Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
examples.flight_status: Flown. Launched 18 June 2009 with LRO and LCROSS (UNH CRaTER on LRO). Current operational status not verified in the sources reviewed.
examples.mass_note: UNH instrument page gives a measured mass of 5.53 kg, with a 6.36 kg allocation. Spaceflight Now (secondary) gives 5.4 kg. The UNH figure is preferred.

power_consumption_w.note: UNH instrument page. Spaceflight Now (secondary) gives an average draw of 7.3 W. The UNH figure is preferred.

examples.dimensions_note: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
examples.configuration: Single integrated sensor and electronics box with simple electronic and mechanical interfaces to the spacecraft.
examples.detector_configuration: Six silicon detectors in thin/thick pairs separated by tissue-equivalent plastic. Thin detectors 140 micrometres; thick detectors 1000 micrometres.

measurement_ranges.high_let_note: As printed on the UNH page the upper bound is below the lower bound; almost certainly a transcription error. Do not use until checked against mission documentation.
measurement_ranges.let_resolution: Better than 0.3% of maximum LET in each range

examples.reported_orbital_dose: CRaTER measured about 0.22 to 0.27 mGy per day in its 50 km orbit, as cited in Wimmer-Schweingruber et al. (2020).

examples.name: Lunar Lander Neutron and Dosimetry (LND) experiment, Chang'e-4 lander
examples.type: Flown lunar-surface radiation dosimeter and neutron detector
examples.flight_status: Flown. Part of the Chang'e-4 lander payload; operated on the lunar surface in the von Karman crater on the lunar far side after landing on 3 January 2019 (Zhang et al., 2020; Wimmer-Schweingruber et al., 2020).
examples.mass_note: Not stated in the sources reviewed (arXiv pre-publication text reviewed does not give a total instrument mass). Take from the published paper or mission documentation before use.
examples.power_note: Not stated in the sources reviewed.
examples.dimensions_note: Not stated in the sources reviewed beyond detector geometry and window size (sensor head window 16 cm x 23 cm).
examples.configuration: Sensor head plus electronics box. The electronics box is housed in the lander's -Y payload compartment; the sensor head is on a bracket close to the upper deck with a re-closeable sky-view window, closed during lunar night to conserve heat. The field of view is approximately 13 degrees from the normal to the lander deck.
examples.detector_configuration: Stack of ten segmented silicon solid-state detectors (SSDs), each with a nominal thickness of 500 micrometres, arranged as a charged-particle telescope. A 20 micrometre gadolinium conversion foil is sandwiched between detector pairs E and F and between G and H for thermal-neutron detection.

measured_surface_result.source: Zhang et al. (2020), Science Advances 6(39), eaaz1334. Abstract read from a copy hosted by the Bexus project.
measured_surface_result.neutral_share_derived: About 23%, derived by dividing the neutral dose rate by the total dose rate; not stated separately in the abstract.
measured_surface_result.measurement_quantity: Absorbed dose in silicon. Not a direct tissue-equivalent dose.
measured_surface_result.dose_equivalent: Not verified against the peer-reviewed paper; a press-reported dose-equivalent figure is not included.

examples.name: Radiation Dose Monitor (RADOM), Chandrayaan-1 orbiter
examples.flight_status: Flown in lunar orbit. Measurements as summarised in Wimmer-Schweingruber et al. (2020).
examples.detector_configuration: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

reported_orbital_measurements.orbit_1: 100 km circular orbit reached 12 November 2008; mean dose rate 0.227 mGy per day over 3545 hours of measurement (20 November 2008 to 18 May 2009).
reported_orbital_measurements.orbit_2: About 200 km (20 May to 28 August 2009); dose rate increased to 0.257 mGy per day.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The three examples differ in platform (orbiter or lander), detector design, measurement quantity (absorbed dose in silicon, dose equivalent, or dose rate in orbit) and period. CRaTER is a single integrated sensor and electronics box on an orbiter; LND is a sensor head and electronics box mounted in a lander payload compartment with a sky-view window; the RADOM physical dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. A new monitor's dimensions would be determined by its detector stack, field-of-view requirement, shielding and mounting interface, and are not generalised here.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is normally expressed in kilograms. Published values in this record are CRaTER 5.53 kg (UNH; Spaceflight Now gives 5.4 kg) and LND not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. RADOM mass is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. Mass affects launch requirements, lander capacity and mounting design.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: CRaTER: 6.66 W typical on the UNH instrument page (allocation 9.00 W); Spaceflight Now gives 7.3 W average. LND and RADOM power values are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A radiation monitor on the Moon must operate in vacuum, under wide temperature swings and under continuous exposure to cosmic and solar radiation. The LND paper states that the lander was modelled to vary from -20 C to +55 C in its operational case, and that the LND electronics box and the lander are expected to lie within that range (Wimmer-Schweingruber et al., 2020). In the LND design, the sensor window is closed during lunar night to conserve heat. For an orbiter, the monitor must tolerate the orbital environment and its field of view must be oriented to the radiation of interest; CRaTER's fields of view are defined in zenith and nadir directions. For a surface monitor, the sensor's field of view depends on lander orientation and local obstructions. The LND paper states that the count rate in a non-isotropic radiation field depends on detector orientation, and that LND's segmented detectors partially compensate for this (Wimmer-Schweingruber et al., 2020). Telemetry must also be planned: CRaTER's stated maximum telemetry rate is 89.1 kbps, and LND sends multi-cadence data products at different intervals.
article.limitations: Sample size and coverage: a single monitor samples one location and one orientation; the LND surface measurement covers one site and one period and does not describe the whole lunar surface. Silicon is not tissue: absorbed dose in silicon does not directly equal absorbed dose in tissue, and converting to dose equivalent depends on quality-factor assumptions (Wimmer-Schweingruber et al., 2020). Neutron measurement: thermal-neutron detection depends on the conversion foil and detector geometry; neutron energies beyond the thermal range need separate analysis. Platform effects: the LND paper notes that the lander's radioisotope thermoelectric generator (RTG) and radioisotope heater units (RHUs) contribute to the radiation environment, and that their effect on the measurements was still being assessed at the time of writing (Wimmer-Schweingruber et al., 2020). Orbital altitude and shadowing: orbital dose rates depend on altitude and on lunar-body shadowing of galactic cosmic rays, as the RADOM values show. Data inconsistencies: some values in secondary sources conflict with primary sources (see limitations_and_uncertainties).

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A radiation environment monitoring package is normally integrated into a spacecraft or lander payload compartment on Earth, launched with the spacecraft, transferred to the Moon and either placed in lunar orbit or installed on the surface.
transportation_process: Orbiter payloads (CRaTER, RADOM): integrate the instrument into the orbiter, launch on a launch vehicle, complete cruise and lunar orbit insertion, then start science operations. CRaTER is a single integrated sensor and electronics box with simple mechanical and electronic interfaces to LRO; UNH gives the LRO and LCROSS launch date as 18 June 2009.

Surface payloads (LND): LND is mounted in the -Y payload compartment of the Chang'e-4 lander, with its sensor head on a bracket near the upper deck with a sky-view window and its electronics box connected to the lander's instrument control unit (Wimmer-Schweingruber et al., 2020). The lander delivered the instrument to the surface and supported its power and data. Integration details are specific to Chang'e-4 and are not transferable to other landers.

Compatibility with other landers: not assessed. A future monitor's compatibility would depend on mass, dimensions, mounting interface, field-of-view requirement, power and data interfaces, and thermal and radiation constraints. No compatibility claim is made.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Orbiter instruments are fixed to the spacecraft and operate in orbit. The LND surface instrument is mounted on the lander and operated as part of the lander's surface operations; the sources reviewed describe no separate deployment mechanism for it.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: CRaTER (LRO, 2009) and RADOM (Chandrayaan-1, 2008 to 2009) are orbital examples; LND (Chang'e-4 lander, 2019) is a surface example. Each is integrated differently and used different interfaces.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Not assessed for any named lander or spacecraft. No compatibility claim is made without verified interface evidence.

article.historical_significance: Radiation measurements around the Moon have been limited. The LND paper cites Chandrayaan-1's RADOM and LRO's CRaTER as the main recent orbital measurements, and notes the Apollo 17 subsurface measurements of low-energy neutrons as the main earlier surface-related data (Wimmer-Schweingruber et al., 2020). The LND surface results are the first direct surface dose measurements reported in the literature reviewed here (Zhang et al., 2020). The examples show a progression from orbital monitoring to surface monitoring, with increasing emphasis on neutrons and on the difference between dose in silicon and dose to tissue.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: 1. Mass, dimensions and power of LND and RADOM are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. CRaTER values come from the UNH instrument page and are contradicted by the Spaceflight Now secondary source. 2. CRaTER high-LET range as printed on the UNH page is internally inconsistent. 3. LND dose-rate units: the Zhang et al. (2020) abstract, as reproduced on a copy hosted by Bexus, gives values in microGy/h. A search summary of a different copy gave Gy/h, which is not physically plausible for lunar surface dose and is treated as a transcription error; confirm against the journal before quoting. 4. LND launch-time statement: the arXiv pre-publication text states the lander and rover were launched at 18:23 on 3 January 2019, while the cited coverage gives 3 January 2019 as the landing date. The launch-time statement appears to be an error and should not be used. 5. Dose equivalent for the LND surface measurement reported in press coverage has not been verified against the peer-reviewed paper and is not included. 6. Current operational status of CRaTER, LND and RADOM beyond the cited data periods is not verified. 7. Images: only one image in this record has a verified direct asset URL; the others are linked references with licence terms not checked. 8. Sources not directly accessed: the Science Advances article and the Space Science Reviews LND article were not fetched in full text; the Science Advances abstract was read from a copy, and the LND technical description from the arXiv pre-publication version.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Only one image has a verified direct asset URL (the UNH-hosted LRO illustration); the other image objects carry image_url null and a linked source page, as the Markdown does.

data_quality_notes: CRaTER mass and power differ between sources: UNH instrument page 5.53 kg and 6.66 W; Spaceflight Now 5.4 kg and 7.3 W average. The UNH figures are used.
CRaTER high-LET range as printed on the UNH page (2.3 to 2.2 keV/um) has a lower bound above its upper bound and is flagged as a probable transcription error.

LND surface dose rate: the Zhang et al. (2020) abstract (via a Bexus copy) gives 13.2 +/- 1 uGy/h total and 3.1 +/- 0.5 uGy/h neutral. A search summary gave Gy/h, treated as a transcription error. Confirm against the journal.

LND arXiv pre-publication text states a launch time of 18:23 on 3 January 2019 for the lander and rover; the cited coverage uses 3 January 2019 as the landing date. The launch-time statement is treated as an error.
LND mass, dimensions and power are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. RADOM mass, dimensions, power and detector configuration are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
The LND dose equivalent reported in press coverage (about 60 microSv/h) was not verified against the peer-reviewed paper and is not included.
Two Markdown image references (LND Kiel photo and lander photo) and the NASA LRO spacecraft callout are linked only; their image_url values are null because no direct asset URL was confirmed.
